newsitem.title: CANADA: Repap tumbles as it searches for buyer.
newsitem.headline: Repap tumbles as it searches for buyer.

text.p: Shares of Repap Enterprises Inc tumbled on Friday on investor worries about the company's financial liquidity after its failed merger deal with Avenor Inc.

Repap was off 0.52 to 0.57 on the Toronto Stock Exchange, topping actives on volume of almost 12 million shares. Analysts said investors were concerned that the company was struggling financially as it sought a new buyer.
"Everybody is shorting the stock," independent analyst John Duncanson said.

Repap officials were unavailable for comment. Company staff said they were in meetings. Analysts said speculation is that Repap officials meeting Friday with potential buyers of part or all of the financially troubled pulp and paper maker.

There are also unconfirmed rumors that Domtar Inc, which had sought a three-way merger with Avenor and Repap last month, remains interested in buying certain Repap assets, possibly in a joint-venture with Finland's UPM-Kymmene Corp. A Domtar official declined to comment, but said the company was not planning an announcement on Friday.
Duncanson said he thinks Repap will find a buyer or buyers for some of its assets if not for all of the company.
"They have good assets, and they are worth more than Repap's debt," Duncanson said.

Repap is struggling with almost C$2.5 billion of debt. Its prize assets are located in Manitoba, New Brunswick and Wisconsin. The New Brunswick and Wisconsin facilities consist of state-of-the-art coated paper printing mills that are largely considered viable operations, Duncanson said.
Repap said on Wednesday that it was reviewing its alternatives to maximize shareholder value.

On March 25, Avenor shareholders, including a Quebec government owned pension fund manager that holds 21 percent of Domtar, massively rejected a proposed C$2.6 billion merger between Avenor and Repap, largely over concerns about the C$3.3 billion of debt the combined companies would carry.

In early March, Repap's British Columbia unit, which analysts say is the weakest of its operating divisions, sought court protection from its creditors under the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act, and was not part of the amended merger proposal between Avenor and Repap.
